title: Scale, Financialization, and the Owned Economy
thesis: More of the economy is being shaped by scale owners, roll-up logic, institutional asset holders, and platform economics that centralize purchasing power, compliance, and capital access
signals: Platform control, roll-ups, and centralized purchasing keep widening the gap.
Workflow software, certification, and managed compliance budgets keep deepening.

Healthcare operators have to absorb this shift in a market where the US dental market, worth $196 billion in 2026, is consolidating rapidly as reimbursement stagnation and workforce shortages push independent practitioners into DSO networks while technology and aging populations provide modest growth.
tensions: Consolidated players can absorb compliance costs and rate risk that squeeze independents; but consolidation also means fewer competitors, tighter coordination, and systemic concentration risk if anchor players fail.
Asset owners (landlords, infrastructure owners, platform operators) keep compounding returns while workers and operators inside the system compete for thinner margins.

title: Physical Reindustrialization and Infrastructure
thesis: The physical economy has become strategic again. Tariffs, reshoring, power demand, logistics, and infrastructure needs are repricing materials, locations, and the trades that make modern buildout possible
signals: Real estate and logistics assets command premium prices; domestic suppliers gain pricing power.
Company mix is already separating, with 1 advantaged examples and 0 exposed examples inside this subtheme set.
Domestic capability, logistics resilience, and buildout bottlenecks matter more in valuation.
tensions: Scale players and capital-rich firms can afford reshoring and power-adjacent land; smaller manufacturers and regional players face margin pressure from tariffs without the resources to relocate.
Power buildout is massive but geographically lumpy—some regions and corridors win spectacularly while others remain peripheral, creating new winners and losers rather than uniform growth.

title: Space, Housing, and Local Friction
thesis: Where Americans live, commute, and locate activity is being reorganized by housing lock-in, office impairment, land scarcity near infrastructure, and the uneven value of local place
signals: Office towers convert to apartments; rural land near power stations attracts investment; logistics parks boom.
Consulting, managed service providers, and independent contractor platforms expand rapidly.
Adaptive reuse, housing lock-in, and power-adjacent land become recurring decision points.
tensions: Office-heavy cities and regions have stranded assets and weakened tax bases, while places with logistics corridors and power access attract capital; but infrastructure builds slowly, and new buildout faces political resistance and environmental scrutiny.

Housing lock-in reduces labor flexibility and pushes up service costs in high-cost areas, but policy options (zoning reform, construction acceleration) remain politically fraught and regionally contested.

title: Machine Intelligence and Compute Buildout
thesis: AI is not just a software feature cycle. It is simultaneously a workflow-compression story, a compute and power infrastructure story, and a market concentration story around who can afford the stack
signals: Companies invest heavily in AI tools and compete for data-center real estate near power sources.
Office towers convert to apartments; rural land near power stations attracts investment; logistics parks boom.
Automation budgets, inference demand, and power-ready site competition keep rising.
tensions: AI productivity gains benefit capital-rich early adopters and scale players; workers in automation-vulnerable roles face wage pressure or displacement, and smaller firms cannot afford the compute or licensing costs that scale players absorb.

Power demand from data centers collides with grid capacity, environmental limits, and local political resistance; buildout is necessary but faces delays and will concentrate infrastructure investment geographically.

title: Work Without the Old Firm
thesis: The traditional firm is thinning. Expertise is rented more often, junior pathways are weaker, benefits are externalized, and automation is increasingly used to defend margins against labor scarcity
signals: Advisory retainers, project staffing, and portable admin layers gain relevance.
Operators lean harder on pricing architecture, pack-size changes, and cost takeout.

Business services operators have to absorb this shift in a market where business coaching in 2025-2026 is shifting from a discretionary C-suite perk to a scaled, AI-augmented professional development tool for mid-market and small-business leaders, underpinned by measured ROI claims and driven by a fragmented but rapidly professionalizing workforce of 165,000+ coaches.
tensions: Companies gain flexibility and margin defense through fractional staffing but lose depth of institutional knowledge and investment in junior development; long-term competitive capability may erode.

Workers gain autonomy in skill selection and portfolio construction but lose stability, benefits continuity, and access to subsidized training; inequality between credential-holders and non-specialists widens.

title: Regulated Software and the Admin State
thesis: A larger share of economic value now comes from managing mandatory complexity: compliance, identity, reimbursement, audit trails, fraud control, privacy, testing, and other workflows customers cannot simply skip
signals: Enterprise spending on governance tools, auditors, and compliance staff accelerates.
Companies shrink portions, bundle aggressively, switch to cheaper materials, and automate labor.
Workflow software, certification, and managed compliance budgets keep deepening.
tensions: Regulatory compliance is a rising cost that hurts smaller, less-integrated players more than scaled incumbents, but it is also a cost that cannot be wished away or automated into nothing—it remains a permanent, defensive business.
The more firms and regulators rely on software and automation to manage compliance, the higher the stakes if that software fails, is breached, or becomes a single point of concentration risk.

title: Aging, Care, and the Assistance Economy
thesis: An older America is creating durable demand across care, insurance, home services, devices, and finance, but labor shortages and payer control determine who actually captures that demand
signals: Demand tilts toward chronic care, assistance, protection, and age-adapted convenience.
Automation, scheduling discipline, retention tactics, and selective simplification accelerate.

Healthcare operators have to absorb this shift in a market where the US home care industry is growing due to an aging population preferring care at home, but faces existential margin compression from stacked payment cuts, severe workforce shortages at 75% annual turnover, and regulatory complexity that is driving consolidation into larger platforms.
tensions: Aging demand is volumetrically massive but economically constrained—payer pressure strips pricing power from providers and device makers, so only scale operators and vertically integrated systems survive.

The caregiver shortage creates both wage pressure that compresses margins and opportunity for automation, home monitoring, and remote care models; operators cannot automate caregiving itself but can optimize dispatch and efficiency.

title: Wellness Recodes Daily Life
thesis: Health behavior is no longer a niche vertical. It is becoming a general operating system for food, drink, beauty, self-presentation, and everyday social decisions
signals: Marketing emphases shift to ingredient transparency, macros, and alignment with personal health goals.
Supply chains pivot to lower-cost regions; premium lines shift downmarket; value-size skus multiply.
Protein, low-sugar, sober-curious, and health-tracking language becomes more central.
tensions: Traditional indulgence categories face volume loss they cannot offset with pricing, while functional and premium alternatives capture margin and cultural prestige.
The line between medical, cosmetic, and wellness spending is disappearing, creating overlap that benefits integrated providers but destabilizes category silos.

title: Barbelled Consumer America
thesis: The old middle of American consumption keeps losing coherence. Households polarize between ruthless value-seeking and selective premium spend, while undifferentiated mid-market operators get squeezed from both sides
signals: Mix shifts toward either obvious value packs or visibly better premium tiers.
Traffic, basket construction, and repeat behavior move toward low-friction channels.

Retail operators have to absorb this shift in a market where the $107.2 billion US discount department stores industry is stabilizing after years of decline, driven by inflation-fueled consumer trade-down behavior and off-price players aggressively expanding, though tariffs and wage pressures are squeezing margins.
tensions: Value leaders win on throughput and scale but face razor margins, while premium players command pricing power but serve smaller, more fickle audiences.

Mid-market retailers are caught between squeezed labor costs and shoppers who now treat their goods as interchangeable, forcing them to either transform into experiential destinations or exit the category altogether.

title: Experience, Status, and Community
thesis: More consumer status is being expressed through participation, memory, aesthetics, and curation rather than through ownership of broad mid-tier goods
signals: Market share concentrates in budget and deluxe segments; mid-tier offerings shrink.
Company mix is already separating, with 1 advantaged examples and 1 exposed examples inside this subtheme set.
Mix shifts toward either obvious value packs or visibly better premium tiers.
tensions: Physical retail venues are becoming economic moats for operators who can program them as discovery environments and brand theaters, while purely transactional retail continues to erode.

Experience-driven spending concentrates wealth and access—not all communities or demographics have equal access to well-programmed venues or travel infrastructure, potentially widening lived inequality.
